content: The combination of fexofenadine and pseudoephedrine is prescribed for adults and children aged 12 years and older to alleviate symptoms of seasonal allergic rhinitis, commonly known as hay fever. These symptoms include a runny nose, sneezing, nasal congestion (stuffy nose), red, itchy, or watery eyes, and itching of the nose, throat, or roof of the mouth. Fexofenadine belongs to a class of medications called antihistamines, which work by blocking the effects of histamine, a substance in the body that triggers allergy symptoms. Pseudoephedrine is classified as a decongestant and works by drying up the nasal passages. This medication is available as an extended-release tablet to be taken orally. The 12-hour tablet is typically taken once or twice daily on an empty stomach with water, while the 24-hour tablet is usually taken once daily on an empty stomach with water. It is recommended to avoid taking this medication with fruit juices such as orange, grapefruit, or apple juice, as they may reduce its effectiveness. It is important to take the medication at the same time(s) every day and follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully. If you have any questions, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Do not take more or less of the medication or take it more frequently than prescribed. This medication helps control the symptoms of seasonal allergic rhinitis but does not cure the condition. Continue taking it even if you feel well and are not experiencing symptoms, as skipping doses may worsen your symptoms. Swallow the tablets whole; do not split, chew, or crush them. This medication may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking fexofenadine and pseudoephedrine, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to fexofenadine (Allegra), pseudoephedrine (Sudafed, in Dimetapp, in Drixoral, and others), any other medications, or any of the ingredients in the tablets. Ask your pharmacist for a list of the ingredients. Do not take this medication if you are currently taking monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors, such as isocarboxazid (Marplan), phenelzine (Nardil), selegiline (Eldepryl), or tranylcypromine (Parnate), or if you have taken them within the past 14 days. Inform your doctor and pharmacist about all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking or plan to take. This includes antibiotics like erythromycin (E-Mycin, Erythrocin), antifungals like ketoconazole (Nizoral), medications for high blood pressure such as methyldopa (Aldomet) and reserpine (Serpalan, Serpasil, Serpatabs), and over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or stimulants. If you are taking an antacid containing aluminum or magnesium (e.g., Maalox, Mylanta), take the antacid a few hours before or after fexofenadine. Inform your doctor if you have glaucoma, difficulty urinating, high blood pressure, or coronary artery disease (a condition where the blood vessels of the heart are narrowed by fat or cholesterol deposits). Also, let your doctor know if you have experienced symptoms such as insomnia, dizziness, weakness, uncontrollable shaking of a body part, or a fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat after taking adrenergic medications like phenylephrine (Neo-Synephrine) or epinephrine (Primatene Mist, EpiPen). Your doctor may advise you not to take fexofenadine and pseudoephedrine. Additionally, inform your doctor if you have or have ever had angina (chest pain or pressure), diabetes, a heart attack, hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid gland), prostatic hypertrophy (enlarged prostate), or heart or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking this medication, contact your doctor immediately. Caffeine-containing beverages (such as coffee, tea, sodas, and energy drinks) may increase restlessness and insomnia caused by pseudoephedrine in sensitive individuals. You may wish to reduce your intake of these beverages. Discuss this with your doctor. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Fexofenadine and pseudoephedrine may cause side effects. Minor side effects include headache, nausea, stomach pain, heartburn, dry mouth, throat irritation, back pain, and pale skin. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects are uncommon but require immediate medical attention. These include nervousness, dizziness, difficulty falling or staying asleep, weakness, fear, anxiety, or tenseness, hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that do not exist), uncontrollable shaking of a body part, seizures, fainting, blurred vision, hives, rash, itching, difficulty breathing or swallowing, swelling of the face, throat, tongue, lips, eyes, hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs, hoarseness, fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat, and difficulty or pain when urinating. If you experience any unusual problems while taking this medication, contact your doctor. Store this medication in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of any outdated or no longer needed medication properly. Consult your pharmacist about the correct disposal method. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Symptoms of overdose may include dizziness, drowsiness, dry mouth, giddiness, headache, nausea, vomiting, sweating, thirst, fast or pounding heartbeat, chest pain, difficulty breathing, difficulty urinating, muscle weakness or tenseness, nervousness, restlessness, difficulty falling or staying asleep, hallucinations (hearing voices or seeing things that do not exist), seizures, or coma. If you are taking the 12-hour tablets, you may notice something that looks like a tablet in your stool. This is simply the empty tablet shell and does not mean you did not receive your full dose of medication. Keep all appointments with your doctor. Do not share your medication with anyone else. If you have questions about refilling your prescription, consult your pharmacist.
